title: Matter of Charter Communications, Inc. v. New York State Tax Appeals Tribunal
court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of New York, Third Department
subject: New York Qualified Emerging Technology Company preferential tax rate — combined group eligibility
summary: The Appellate Division affirmed the New York Tax Appeals Tribunal's determination that every member of a combined corporate group must independently qualify as a Qualified Emerging Technology Company (QETC) — a status tied to New York's incentive for private investment in research and development and emerging technology industries — before the group can claim the reduced QETC corporate franchise tax rate.

body.text: Charter Communications and its combined affiliates (formerly Time Warner Cable) filed combined New York franchise tax returns for the 2012 through 2014 tax years, self-identifying as a 'qualified emerging technology company' and paying the reduced tax rate available to qualified New York manufacturers under Tax Law section 210. Following an audit, the Department of Taxation and Finance determined that Charter did not qualify because certain members of the combined group were not located in New York during the years at issue, and assessed a deficiency of $7,805,767.54.
QETC Status as a Vehicle for Incentivizing R&D Investment

The court explained that the QETC preferential rate traces to the 1998 New York State Emerging Industry Jobs Act, through which the Legislature declared its intent to incentivize 'private investments in research and development and in emerging technology industries' in New York, in recognition of 'significant barriers to the commercialization of scientific and technological discoveries by emerging technology firms.' A QETC is defined, in relevant part, as a company located in New York whose primary products or services are classified as emerging technologies.
'Taxpayer' Means Each Corporation, Not the Combined Group

Applying de novo review to this question of statutory interpretation, the Appellate Division agreed with the Tax Appeals Tribunal that the statutory text unambiguously defines a 'taxpayer' as each individual corporation subject to tax, not the combined group as a whole. Because the QETC definition — including its requirement that the company be 'located in New York' — attaches to the 'taxpayer,' every member of a combined group filing together must independently satisfy the QETC criteria, including having a New York location, for the group to receive the reduced rate. The court rejected Charter's proposed alternative of applying the reduced rate only to those individual members that separately qualified, holding this would effectively decombine the group and distort its reported New York economic activity.

The court also rejected Charter's dormant Commerce Clause challenge, finding the statutory scheme did not discriminate against interstate commerce given that out-of-state affiliates could still qualify by demonstrating a real property connection to New York.
The Appellate Division confirmed the Tax Appeals Tribunal's determination and dismissed Charter's petition.

Significance: This decision resolved a threshold eligibility rule with major consequences for any multi-entity technology or telecommunications group filing combined New York returns while seeking QETC treatment, and it was subsequently applied by the Division of Tax Appeals in Matter of Fidelity National Information Services Inc. and Subsidiaries.
